articles.title: Trump Endorses U.S. Tax Incentive to Keep Hollywood Production: ‘Let’s Get This Done!’
articles.summary: President Trump on Monday endorsed a federal tax incentive for film and TV production, a move long sought by Hollywood studios and unions. In a statement posted to Truth Social, Trump said he will push for a bipartisan bill to save the industry.
body: Several Democratic lawmakers have gotten behind the idea, notably including Sen. Adam Schiff, who held a hearing on the topic in March. But Schiff and others have said that Republican lawmakers were waiting on a positive signal from the White House getting on board.
Charles Rivkin, the CEO of the Motion Picture Association, applauded Trump’s move in a statement.

“For over a century, American studios, casts, and crews have produced the films and series that the world wants to see,” Rivkin said. “A federal incentive would be a landmark step toward bringing more production to local communities in all 50 states, strengthening our nation’s economy, and making our country a more competitive place to produce, create, and tell great stories. We applaud President Trump’s support for this vital action, and we look forward to continuing to work with the White House and bipartisan leaders in Congress to enact a meaningful and effective national incentive into law.”

Supporters of the measure have cited a dramatic drop in domestic production since the streaming bubble burst in 2022. Around 73,000 jobs have been lost nationwide, about two-thirds of them in Los Angeles.

articles.title: ‘Gargoyles’ Live-Action Series Not Moving Forward at Disney+
articles.summary: The live-action “Gargoyles” reboot has turned to stone. The project, which was in early development at Disney+, is no longer moving forward, a source confirms to Variety.
body: Dauberman (“It”) would have served as writer and executive producer of “Gargoyles” 2.0 with Wan also executive producing. Disney Branded Television was attached as the studio. The logline for the project read: “Based on the cult classic Disney animated series, Goliath is the last of a heroic race of gargoyle warriors who once lived among mankind. Free from a centuries long curse that turned him into stone, Goliath struggles to solve the mystery of his past while watching over modern-day New York City alongside police detective Elisa Maza.”

The original “Gargoyles” hailed from Walt Disney Television Animation and was considered dark for the Mouse House. The show followed a fantastical species known as gargoyles, who are made of stone during the day but come alive at night. When a clan of gargoyles living in Scotland in the late 10th century are betrayed and cursed by a magic spell, they cannot break from their stone sleep until a thousand years later in modern New York, thanks to the intervention of a wealthy industrialist named David Xanatos. The gargoyles decide to claim New York as their new home and vow to protect it.

articles.title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
articles.summary: The singer, 21, will be now represented by a public defender in the murder trial of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez. He has pleaded not guilty.
body: The celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case.

The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.
Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday.
A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body.

articles.title: Writer and Comedian Marty Nadler Dies at 80
articles.summary: Marty Nadler, a producer, sitcom writer and stand-up comedian, who worked on “Happy Days,” “Laverne and Shirley” and “The Odd Couple,” died in Margate, Florida, on Aug. 26. He was 80. His son, Charlie Nadler, said he died due to complications from myasthenia gravis.
body: Nadler’s son followed in his footsteps, and they performed stand-up together around the country. They recently recorded their act at The Garry Marshall Theatre in Los Angeles titled “A Boomer and A Millennial Walk Into a Special.” It will be released in early 2027 by Comedy Dynamics. “It was a magical evening with family, friends, and colleagues from all chapters of dad’s life in attendance,” Charlie Nadler said.
Nadler is survived by his ex-wife, with whom he remained close friends; their son Charlie and daughter-in-law Cary Kandel. Nadler will be interred on Martha’s Vineyard.

articles.title: ‘Sometimes you just need a good cry’: why Little Women is my feelgood movie
articles.summary: The latest in our series of writers highlighting their go-to comfort films is an ode to the teary 1994 adaptation of the classic novel. I have an ongoing argument with some friends about how I refuse to watch Interstellar again, despite considering it a beautiful and well-crafted film.
body: But at the same time, the movie I choose as my feelgood film is one that has reduced me to a sobbing, snotty mess time and time again, whether I’m watching it curled up with my cat on the couch, swaddled in blankets while sick in bed or jostling with my seatmate for the armrest on an airplane. And just like with the score from Interstellar, the moment I hear Thomas Newman’s wistful little oboe intro of the 1994 version of Little Women, I can feel my eyes well up with tears.

As you’ve probably discerned already, I tend to feel things very strongly. Probably one of my most psychotic traits is that I have to spoil the endings of most movies before I watch them for the first time because if I get too attached to a character and that character dies, it could take me several days to recover. But sometimes you just need a good cry, and that’s exactly what Gillian Armstrong’s Little Women is for me.

I have an ongoing argument with some friends about how I refuse to watch Interstellar again, despite considering it a beautiful and well-crafted film.

But sometimes you just need a good cry, and that’s exactly what Gillian Armstrong’s Little Women is for me.

articles.title: Victoria Beckham's company makes its first profit after 18 years
articles.summary: Beckham's fashion and beauty business makes a £7.3m operating profit after years of losses.
body: Victoria Beckham's fashion and beauty business has made an operating profit for the first time since she founded it in 2008, the company has said.
Victoria Beckham Holdings Ltd, which is led by the former Spice Girl as creative director, made an operating profit of £7.3m in 2025, accounts show, after years of losses.
"We have all worked hard for a long time for this moment of profitability and growth," Lady Beckham told the Financial Times, external.

"We've been very transparent about the problems that we had in the business but have recovered and are now growing at a sensible pace. After 20 years, people don't look at my brand as a celebrity brand any more."

articles.title: Bel review – the powerful life force and haunting absence of a traumatised singer-songwriter
articles.summary: Beldina Odenyo alchemised the pain of exile, loss and racism into music as Heir of the Cursed before her death in 2021, as this attentive tribute explores. Instead of an artist in a booth, a lone amplifier plays the music of singer-songwriter Beldina Odenyo for a cluster of microphones to pick up…
body: Performing under the moniker Heir of the Cursed, a translation of the Tetela name of assassinated Congolese leader Patrice Lumumba, Odenyo was on the verge of bigger recognition at the end of 2021 after a successful performance at Edinburgh’s Usher Hall. But hemmed in by successive Covid lockdowns, the 31-year-old is clearly unwell in a discomfiting backstage interview. Squirming, monosyllabic, she seems to be regressing to the non-verbal state of shock in which she arrived in Dumfriesshire from Kenya as a young child.

articles.title: Trump Calls for Passage of Federal Film and TV Tax Incentive: “Let’s Get This Done!”
articles.summary: The bill already had bipartisan support, but Republican lawmakers especially seemed to be waiting to see if the President would support the idea.
body: For some time now, the idea of a federal film and television tax incentive has had bipartisan support, but Republican lawmakers have seemingly been waiting on word from the White House.

Now, it appears, that word has come. On Monday, President Donald Trump posted that he wants to “get this done“ in a lengthy Truth Social message expressing support for the idea of a federal tax credit.

The president added, “Meetings are being set up with the Leaders of both Parties in order to get this done. It should be Bipartisan, especially since so much money is being lost in California, and other largely Blue States. I am going to suggest that Republicans and Democrats get together, and immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America.”

The president then exhorted Congress to approve such legislation, which would provide films and TV shows that shoot in the U.S. with incentives that they could stack on top of individual states’ tax credits. “What we watch on the Silver Screen should be made in what was once the Movie and Motion Picture Capital of the World. Let’s get this done!” Trump concluded.
points: The bill already had bipartisan support, but Republican lawmakers especially seemed to be waiting to see if the President would support the idea.

articles.title: ‘The whistling on the theme tune? That’s Dickie Attenborough!’ Hayley Mills on Whistle Down the Wind
articles.summary: ‘I’d just made two films in America. Shooting on a Lancashire farm was very different. There was mud everywhere – and we’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in buns’ Whistle Down the Wind was originally a novel written by my mother, Mary Hayley Bell, about three children living on a…
body: Dickie Attenborough thought it was a wonderful story, and convinced my parents it should be made into a film by the production company he’d set up with the actor and writer Bryan Forbes. After the original director, Guy Green, pulled out, Bryan took over at the 11th hour. He’d never directed before. When Dickie asked if he could do it, he apparently said: “I’ve no idea. We’ll soon find out!”

Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall were engaged as writers and made the brilliant decision to move the story to a remote part of Lancashire. The perfect location was found in the village of Downham, at the foot of Pendle Hill, famous for the witch hunts. Nearly all of the children in the film were local: the only experienced child actors were Roy Holder, who played Jackie, and me. I was 14 and a head and shoulders taller than most of the other kids. The sleeves on my coat were too short and my arms stuck out like a scarecrow’s.
